title: [Autour de La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois, pages 1 à 67] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: K is a field of finite type over Q, Γ = Gal(K̄/K), and U is a smooth geometrically connected curve over K of type (g,ν). The arithmetic fundamental group sits in (1) 1 → π = π_1(U_K̄) → 𝓔_U → Γ → 1. The previous page notes that rational points give sections of (1), with U(K) → {π-conjugacy classes of sections} injective. The aim is to find other 'geometric' sources of sections, the first step toward the section conjecture for affine curves.

At a K-rational cusp i, the loop around the puncture gives an inertia subgroup L_i ⊂ π, with L_i ≅ T_∞(K̄*) = Ẑ(1) =: T. Its centralizer Z(L_i) in 𝓔_U (in modern terms the decomposition group D_i) is an extension (2) 1 → L_i → Z(L_i) → Γ → 1. Splittings of (2) exist, e.g. one defined by choosing a uniformizer at i in the completed local ring Ô_{Û,i}. The conjugacy classes of splittings of (2) form a torsor under H^1(Γ,T). By Kummer theory, (3) H^1(Γ,T) ≅ lim_n H^1(K,μ_n) ≅ lim_n K*/K*^n = (K*)^. This torsor maps injectively into the π-conjugacy classes of sections of (1). In modern terms, this is the 'packet of cuspidal sections' at i, a (K*)^-torsor.

Proposition: (a) if (g,ν) ≠ (0,0),(0,1), i.e. π ≠ 1, the cuspidal sections are distinct from the sections coming from points of U(K); (b) if moreover (g,ν) ≠ (0,2), i.e. in the anabelian case, the packets attached to distinct cusps i1 ≠ i2 are disjoint.

The margin and the next page sketch the proof: 'fill the hole' i, so the cuspidal section becomes the point section of the rational point i on U' = U ∪ {i}, and one uses injectivity for U'. The case (0,3) is the exception, since filling two holes leads to type (0,1), where no injectivity result is available. For that case Grothendieck invokes a conjectured fixed-point statement, π^{Γ'} = L_i, which he calls 'hautement plausible' and lists among the key questions.
errors: Part (a) of the Proposition is false as stated for type (0,2). For U = G_m we have π = Ẑ(1) abelian, so L_i = π and Z(L_i) = 𝓔_U. The cuspidal packet at 0 (or ∞) is then the whole (K*)^-torsor of sections of (1), and it contains the sections coming from rational points t ∈ K*. Claim (a) needs the hyperbolic hypothesis, i.e. the exclusion of (0,2) as well. This matches the proof strategy: filling one hole of G_m gives A^1, of type (0,1), where injectivity is unavailable. Grothendieck excludes (0,2) only for part (b).

The torsor statement should concern splittings of (2), not (1). Also, the group is H^1(Γ,T) (continuous cohomology with the cyclotomic action), not Hom(Γ,T), since Γ acts nontrivially on T. The handwriting 'HM' is most plausibly H^1. The limit identification also tacitly uses lim^1 of the finite groups μ_n(K) vanishing, which is fine.

The plausible auxiliary statement on the next page, π^{Γ'} = L_i, cannot be literally a fixed-point statement for a Γ'-action through a section. Γ' acts on L_i ≅ Ẑ(1) by the cyclotomic character, so L_i^{Γ'} = 1. It must be read as a centralizer/normalizer-type statement (e.g. the centralizer of an open subgroup of the decomposition group lies in L_i). This is ambiguous on these pages.

ideas.what: Inertia/decomposition subgroup at a rational cusp, D_i = Z(L_i), as an extension of Γ by L_i ≅ Ẑ(1)
ideas.usually_credited_to: standard (Grothendieck SGA1 tame theory; used by Nakamura, Tamagawa, Mochizuki in anabelian geometry)
ideas.where_published: Tame fundamental group in SGA1/Grothendieck–Murre; not this specific use

ideas.what: Sections of π_1(U) → Γ arising from splittings of the decomposition group at a cusp, forming a torsor under H^1(K,Ẑ(1)) = (K*)^ via a choice of uniformizer
ideas.modern_name: packets of cuspidal sections (sections at infinity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Grothendieck (letter to Faltings, section conjecture for affine curves); worked out by Nakamura, Stix (Rational points and arithmetic of fundamental groups, LNM 2054), Esnault–Hai
ideas.where_published: Letter to Faltings 1983 discusses the section conjecture; whether it details cuspidal packets is unsure

ideas.what: Cuspidal sections are distinct from rational-point sections, and packets at distinct cusps are disjoint for hyperbolic curves, proved by filling punctures and reducing to injectivity for the completed curve
ideas.modern_name: disjointness of cuspidal packets / injectivity of the section map including cusps

ideas.what: Conjectured 'π^{Γ'} = L_i' (centralizer/fixed points of an open Galois subgroup acting through the cuspidal decomposition group lie in the inertia), flagged as a key question
ideas.modern_name: centralizers of decomposition groups / commensurator of cuspidal decomposition groups

missed.claim: Early (pre-Faltings-letter era, c.1981) explicit description of cuspidal section packets as (K*)^-torsors, with a proposition on their disjointness from point sections and from each other. The (0,3) case is singled out as requiring an extra centralizer statement. This is historically early but now standard (Nakamura, Stix).
missed.quote: L'ens. des classes de conjugaison scindages ... est un torseur sous H^1(Γ,T) ≃ lim Hom(K,μ_n) ≃ \widehat{K^*}
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Documents Grothendieck's priority for the cuspidal-section part of the affine section conjecture. It also shows the (0,3) case identified as the delicate one.

deep.surprise_reason: The content (cuspidal packets as (K*)^-torsors and their disjointness) is now standard in the section-conjecture literature, but it is an early unpublished formulation by Grothendieck. There is also a small genuine slip: the (0,2) case should be excluded from the first claim.
transcription_corrections: 'Hom(Γ,T)' in (3) should read H^1(Γ,T) (written 'HM'). Likewise 'Hom(K,μ_n)' should read H^1(K,μ_n).
The torsor statement refers to splittings of (2) (the numeral appears overwritten); mathematically it must be (2).
Line 1 is likely a continuation describing L_i (a loop group around the cusp i) defined up to conjugation. The reading 'E_{\bar K,K}' is uncertain.
Margin reads roughly: '(c'est évident sauf pour type (0,3)), [pour lequel] vérifié en admettant...'.
The final line reads '... pour deux indices i=i_1 et i=i_2 distincts, sont distinctes.'
